At balances and rates as of 9 November 2026, the changes add about $3.5M of annualised revenue to the DAO and raise the blended RF from 12.0% to 12.7%. The proposal is part of the ongoing effort to streamline Aave V3. Motivation Overview Over the past months, the DAO has been streamlining Aave V3. Low-adoption reserves and instances have been wound down, Aave V2 has been frozen, and ongoing work aims to focus Ethereum Core on liquid, bluechip collateral, with assets that carry additional risk moving to Aave V4, where that risk can be priced. This proposal applies the same direction to the protocol’s revenue side. Every borrowable reserve exposes the DAO to collateral, oracle and liquidation risk. The RF compensates the DAO for carrying that risk. On many reserves today, the DAO keeps a small share of the interest on positions whose tail risk it fully underwrites. This will future-proof Ethereum’s leading position as the credible decentralized root of trust for the global economy, with ETH as the programmable store of value at its center. Being post-quantum is not enough, we intend on being post-AI too. AI capabilities are taking off: quantum timelines are moving forward, AI is solving open maths problems that pose the question whether some cryptographic primitives might break, and it’s finding software vulnerabilities at scale. Ethereum is uniquely positioned for this moment and leading the way : years of prior research and work have produced a clear plan to become post-quantum and plausibly post-AI, and now we should make it the priority. The network is resilient through its decentralized validator set and client diversity, and formal verification is already deeply embedded into its core development process. pqai27 means rethinking upcoming hardforks , including Hegotá: anything not on the critical path to pqai should be reconsidered. events.excerpt: A group of privacy enthusiasts discovered on Tuesday that the default software development kit (SDK) that wallet apps use to connect to Ledger hardware devices transmits details regarding crypto transaction signatures to Ledger servers. When the discovery spread on social media, privacy proponents were surprised to discover that Ledger crypto wallet apps have been quietly broadcasting transaction details to Ledger. The behavior has been a default since Ledger’s context-module version 1.16, i.e. since May 2026 or earlier. It was a devastating discovery for users who have mistakenly thought the default behavior of Ledger wallets was private signing and private broadcasts of transactions directly to blockchain networks. Unfortunately, many Ledger wallets have been simultaneously doxxing personal details to the world’s largest hardware wallet manufacturer. Substantial metadata has been transmitting from Ledger devices to Ledger servers since late May. Apps and users must opt-out of this information-sharing behavior when using wallet apps, and the overwhelming majority do not. events.excerpt: Hi everyone. I’m Leandro, a full-stack developer and open-source contributor with experience in AI, blockchain, web and mobile development, and developer tooling. I recently submitted a grant proposal for Zcash Wallet Devtools , an open-source toolkit designed to improve the developer experience when building applications with Zcash. What’s the idea? Integrating Zcash wallets and payment requests into web applications can be challenging to debug. Developers often need to rely on console logs, manually inspect SDK responses, and troubleshoot different wallet behaviors. I’d like to make that process easier by building a lightweight, privacy-aware debugging toolkit inspired by tools like React Query Devtools and Solana’s Connector Debugger. What will it include? TypeScript SDK: Instrumentation for wallet connections, events, state changes, and errors. Interactive Devtools Dashboard: A visual panel that runs inside applications during development. ZIP-321 Diagnostics: Inspect payment request lifecycle events and troubleshoot integration issues. Privacy-Aware Logging: Protect sensitive wallet information by default. Wallet Integration: Initial support for one compatible Zcash wallet SDK. Next.js Demo: A working example showing how everything integrates. Bilingual Documentation: Techni
events.headline: Zcash Wallet Devtools - Privacy-Aware Debugging Toolkit for Web Developers

events.excerpt: ERC-3668 (CCIP-Read) lets a contract hand a read off to a gateway, but the gateway either has to be trusted or has to return a proof the contract can verify. For many cross-chain reads a valid proof cannot be produced. That does not make the read unsafe, because the client usually already trusts its own RPC connection to the other chain and could simply make the call itself. ERC-8446 lets the client act as the gateway. The contract reverts with OffchainLookup as usual, with an x-chain URL that names the chain and contract to read, and the client calls that contract with its own RPC and passes the result to the callback exactly as eth_call returns it. No third party is involved. The chain and address are encoded as an ERC-7930 Interoperable Address, for example USDC on Base. x-chain:0x0001000002210514833589fcd6edb6e08f4c7c32d4f71b54bda02913 An optional ?finalized=true makes the read at the finalized block instead of the latest one. The client alone decides whether it can safely read a given chain, and never takes RPC endpoints from the contract. Nested x-chain lookups are not followed, so each call makes at most one cross-chain hop. Contracts can also tell when a client does not support the ERC. They add a data: URL after the x-chain URL, which only older clients reach, and it del
events.headline: ERC-8446: Cross-Chain Client Gateway for CCIP-Read

events.excerpt: ERC-8048 and ERC-8049 store metadata onchain as key-value pairs, but a JSON document has no compact way to point at those values. A URL that names the contract, the chain, and the token ID repeats what the client already knows and differs for every token. ERC-8493 defines the onchain URI scheme. The contract and token ID are not written in the URI, they come from the function that returned the document. { "image": "onchain:image/png", "thumbnail": { "small": "onchain:image/png?key=thumb.small" } } onchain:image/png is 17 bytes and works unchanged for every token. When the URI comes from tokenURI or uri , the client reads it with metadata(tokenId, key) from ERC-8048, and when it comes from contractURI , with metadata(key) from ERC-8049. A direct member of the top-level document uses its own name as the key, and everywhere else the key parameter names it. Tokens that are already deployed can use the scheme by adding a metadata_contract property to their JSON, which points the client at a separate metadata contract. Linked JSON documents keep the same contract and token, so the whole thing reads as one data tree. The scheme adds no contract surface. Existing ERC-8048 and ERC-8049 contracts support it with no change, and a client that does not know the scheme sees a URI it can ignore
events.headline: ERC-8493: Onchain URI Scheme

events.excerpt: Summary LlamaRisk is building Aave’s Risk Layer: automated risk solutions that make expert risk judgment verifiable, with every parameter, bound and action checkable onchain. The Aave Risk Framework set this direction in June by making continuous risk oracles part of the protocol’s standing infrastructure. Governance and manual review can trail a fast-moving event by hours, and the evolution of AI capabilities keeps shortening the time between finding a weakness and exploiting it, so protection has to run continuously and at machine speed. LlamaGuard PT went live in September as the first of these solutions. We continue the rollout with LlamaGuard Caps as the next addition. Aave’s greatest strength is its liquidity, deep enough to move capital instantly and at scale. Defending access to that liquidity programmatically protects Aave’s users, even when a failure elsewhere in DeFi puts compromised collateral or stolen assets in play. LlamaGuard Caps hardens Aave’s perimeter. Its first stage, a borrow rate limiter for Aave V3, gives each reserve a margin of borrowing room above its debt, sized to the reserve. These entanglements include a controversial video-streaming platform that platforms right-wing influencers, royalties from gold mines, satellites, and a BTC treasury play. Protos has reviewed regulatory filings in the US to better understand Tether’s links to these public markets. Map showing Tether’s connections to various publicly-traded firms. Video-streaming for Donald Trump Jr. Rumble (Nasdaq: RUM) is a video-streaming platform that partners with Donald Trump Jr. to stream his podcast, Triggered. Tether has a 50.3% stake in Rumble, counting its warrants. However, Tether doesn’t truly have control of Rumble, deliberately staying under 9.9% voting control. Chart showing Rumble’s price. Rumble also had previously acquired Tether-owned Northern Data. This firm has started advertising itself as an “AI infrastructure and video company” as it widens its focus from just doing video streaming, effectively splitting itself in half (still under the RUM Group parent), with Rumble maintaining the video platform and Quake AI leading the cloud and AI business. Tether is the most important purchaser of advertising from Rumble, according to Rumble’s 10-Q
events.headline: Tether has about $4.8B in exposure to US stock markets

events.excerpt: Props 1060 and 1061, IBC joining LF Decentralized Trust, ATOM on Paxos, remote signers, and a delegation program update The following is a recap of the November 11, 2026 Cosmos Hub validator call. These calls occur once per month, and recaps like this one are posted on the Cosmos Hub forums following each call. The call covered the result of Prop 1060 and the open vote on Prop 1061, IBC joining LF Decentralized Trust, ATOM on Paxos and the Blockworks TTF filing, remote signers and Cosmos KMS, and a change to how commission is checked in the delegation program. Last month’s recap is on the forum, and the slides from this call are available to view. Prop 1060: the community pool’s USDC.n is now USDC.inj Prop 1060 passed on November 3, and the funds were back in the community pool as USDC.inj on November 4. The community pool did not have a mechanism to do the swap by itself, so the proposal was a community pool spend that sent the full USDC.n balance to a DAODAO multisig of six community members and validators, which executed the swap and sent the funds back. The 566,067.06 USDC.n was swapped to USDC.inj in two tranches through DAODAO proposals posted publicly ahead of the vote and returned in full on November 4 . Thank you to everyone who helped make that a success. Circle pauses
events.headline: Cosmos Hub Validator Call: Recap - Nov 11, 2026
